pos: n. pl. (those who help alongside another; co-workers in a common cause)
etymology: A compound of fellow (Old Norse felagi, one who lays down a fee with another, a partner) and helper. The Greek is sunergos, a fellow worker, from sun (with) and ergon (work).
biblical_def: John writes to Gaius about the itinerant preachers who had come through, and gives the reason the church must support them: “We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth” (3 John 1:8). A fellowhelper is one who works alongside, and the striking thing in this verse is the object: not fellowhelpers to the preachers, but to the truth. The hospitality Gaius showed was not patronage of men but partnership with a message. He had done it already: “Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers” (3 John 1:5). The doctrine is important because it dignifies the sender as truly as the sent. The man who lodges and funds a preacher is not a spectator to gospel work; he is a fellow worker in it, and he will share its reward. Paul uses the same category of himself toward the Corinthians, refusing any lordship over their faith: “Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand” (2 Corinthians 1:24). Ministry in the New Testament is a fellowship of labour under one Lord, never a clerical caste with an audience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FELLOW-HELPER, a coadjutor; one who helps or assists along with another.
webster_full: FELLOW-HELPER, n. A coadjutor; one who assists with another.
FELLOW, n. An associate; a companion; one united with another in the same business.
HELPER, n. One that helps, aids or assists; an assistant.
Greek sunergos, a fellow worker, from sun, with, and ergon, work.

Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand.
corruption_summary: Gospel labour is divided into professionals who do the work and laymen who fund it, so that the supporting believer is treated as a donor rather than a fellow worker with the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors shelter behind this verse. The clerical error treats ordained men as the ministry and the rest of the church as its audience and revenue; the consumer error treats the congregation as customers who purchase religious services and may withhold payment when displeased. Both deny what John says, that the man who receives a preacher becomes a fellowhelper to the truth itself.

The New Testament gives real authority to elders and real honour to the office, and the dictionary holds the two offices of elder and deacon with a plurality of elders as the apostolic pattern. But Paul will not call that authority dominion over faith, and John will not call Gaius a patron. The sender labours with the sent. That is why the household that opens its door, the woman who feeds the itinerant, and the church that funds the missionary are not supporting the work; they are doing it.

pos: n. pl. (fellow labourers; those who work together in a common task)
etymology: A compound of fellow and worker. The Greek is again sunergos, a fellow worker, from sun (with) and ergon (work), the same word rendered fellowhelpers in 3 John.
biblical_def: Closing the letter to Colossae, Paul names the handful of Jewish believers still standing with him in Rome: “And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Colossians 4:11). Fellowworkers is the plain English for sunergoi, and the phrase unto the kingdom of God defines the work. These men were not Paul's employees or his admirers; they laboured toward the same end he laboured toward. The word only is poignant. The great apostle, writing from prison, counts his Jewish co-labourers on the fingers of one hand, and adds that they have been a comfort to him. The same chapter shows what such work looked like in practice: “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God” (Colossians 4:12). Fervent prayer is named as labour. John's word to Gaius completes the picture: hospitality to a preacher makes a man a fellowhelper to the truth (3 John 1:8).

webster_full: FELLOW-WORKER, n. One employed in the same work or business with another.
FELLOW, n. An associate; a companion; a partner in business.
WORKER, n. One that works; one that labors.

We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.
corruption_summary: Ministry is measured by platform and visible scale, so that unnamed intercessors and small companies of faithful labourers are not counted as workers at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul's little list quietly teaches: the kingdom of God is advanced by a small number of named and mostly obscure labourers, and prayer is reckoned among the heaviest of their labours.

Modern evangelical culture counts influence. Audience, reach, platform and scale are the measures, and a man labouring fervently in prayer for a congregation he cannot visit registers as nothing. Paul closes his letter the other way round. He names Justus, Aristarchus, Mark and Epaphras; he says these only are my fellowworkers; and he singles out the praying man for particular commendation. A church that learns to count as Paul counts will honour its intercessors and its few faithful co-labourers as the real workforce of the kingdom.

pos: n. (completeness, maturity, the state in which a thing is whole)
etymology: From perfect, Latin perficere, to carry through to completion, with the suffix -ness. The Greek is teleiotes, completeness or maturity, from telos, an end or goal.
biblical_def: Having listed the graces the Colossians are to put on, Paul names the one that holds the rest together: “And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness” (Colossians 3:14). Perfectness is not flawlessness but completeness; the Greek teleiotes means a thing brought to its proper end. Charity is called the bond, the girdle that binds the whole garment of graces into one. Strip love out and the preceding virtues come apart into separate and brittle pieces: mercy without love becomes condescension, meekness without love becomes timidity, forbearance without love becomes mere endurance. The verse immediately before supplies the wardrobe: “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Colossians 3:12). And Paul's great chapter on charity ends by ranking it above even the two graces that abide with it: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13). Perfectness, then, is a Christian fully clothed and belted; the dictionary's doctrine of progressive sanctification, worked by the Spirit in the elect.

corruption_summary: Perfectness is taken either as a sinless state attainable in this life or as love detached from the law, so that the bond is kept and the garment it was meant to bind is discarded.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors press on this word from opposite sides. Wesleyan and later holiness teaching read perfectness as entire sanctification, a second blessing in which sin is eradicated in this life; the Reformed confessions deny it, holding that the regenerate are sanctified progressively and that remaining corruption abides until glory. The Greek teleiotes means maturity, not the absence of sin.

The opposite error is more common now. Charity is kept as the one surviving Christian virtue and then set against God's commandments, so that love becomes the warrant for setting aside what Scripture forbids. Paul will not allow it. Charity is a bond, and a bond must have something to bind: the mercies, kindness, humbleness, meekness and longsuffering of the verse before, and behind them the whole moral law. Love is the belt of the garment, never a substitute for it.

pos: n. (lowliness; the state of mind that thinks rightly low of itself)
etymology: From humble, Latin humilis, low, from humus, the ground, with the suffix -ness. The Greek is tapeinophrosune, lowliness of mind, a compound word the New Testament effectively coined as a virtue.
biblical_def: In the Colossian list of garments the believer puts on, the third item is humbleness of mind: “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Colossians 3:12). The Greek tapeinophrosune was not a virtue in the pagan world; lowliness was the condition of a slave and a thing to be escaped, and the New Testament takes the word and makes it an ornament of the elect. The phrase of mind matters: this is not a manner but a judgment, a settled estimate of oneself in the light of God. Micah had long since bound it to the whole duty of man: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8). Paul gives the test by which it is known: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Philippians 2:3), a verse whose next paragraph is the descent of the Son of God from glory to a cross. Christian humbleness is grounded in Christ's, and clothed on men whom God has already named holy and beloved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): HUMBLENESS, the state of being humble or low; humility; freedom from pride.
webster_full: HUMBLENESS, n. The state of being humble or low; humility.

corruption_summary: Humbleness is recast as low self-esteem to be cured, or counterfeited as a performance of modesty, when Scripture means a true estimate of oneself before God.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic culture cannot easily distinguish humility from self-contempt, and so treats lowliness of mind as a deficit to be repaired by affirmation. On that account Colossians 3:12 prescribes the disease. The confusion is real, and the answer is not to defend self-contempt: a man who grovels is as absorbed in himself as a man who boasts. Scriptural humbleness is not a low opinion of oneself but a true one, held by a man who has been told by God that he is elect, holy and beloved.

The opposite counterfeit is humility as performance, the studied self-deprecation that fishes for contradiction. Paul gives a test that defeats both: in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. That cannot be faked for long and cannot be practised by the self-absorbed. And its ground is the mind of Christ, who being in the form of God made Himself of no reputation.

pos: n. (openness, freedom of speech; the quality of being clear and unconcealed)
etymology: From plain, Latin planus, flat, level, clear, with the suffix -ness. The Greek is parrhesia, from pan (all) and rhesis (speech): speaking everything, boldness and openness of utterance.
biblical_def: Comparing his ministry with Moses' veiled face, Paul draws the conclusion: “Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech” (2 Corinthians 3:12). The Greek parrhesia means all-speech, the liberty to say the whole thing without veil or reserve. Moses covered his face; the new covenant minister does not, because the hope he carries is open and the glory he serves is unfading. Plainness therefore belongs to the gospel's very nature, not to any one man's temperament. Paul spells out its negative side: “But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God” (2 Corinthians 4:2). And he had already refused the rhetorical arts that trade in impressiveness: “And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4). Plain preaching is thus a doctrinal requirement. A veiled gospel is a contradiction, and a minister who obscures is not being profound but unfaithful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PLAINNESS, openness; rough sincerity; frankness; freedom from ornament or disguise; artlessness.
webster_full: PLAINNESS, n. Openness; rough sincerity; frankness; as plainness of speech.

And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
corruption_summary: Deliberate vagueness in the pulpit is dignified as humility or nuance, while clear statement of what Scripture says is treated as arrogance or a failure of tone.
corruption_paragraphs: A ministry under cultural pressure learns to speak in a register that cannot be quoted. Hard doctrines are gestured at rather than stated; sin is described in categories broad enough to accuse nobody; the sermon ends where the application should begin. The vagueness is defended as epistemic modesty or pastoral sensitivity, and plainness is recoded as a lack of charity.

Paul puts plainness on the other side of the ledger entirely. Craftiness and handling the word of God deceitfully are what he renounces; manifestation of the truth to every man's conscience is what he practises. He is not commending bluntness of manner, for the same apostle became all things to all men and wept over those he warned. He is forbidding a veiled gospel. If the new covenant has no veil, the preacher may not supply one.

pos: adv. (in a holy manner; piously, with separation unto God)
etymology: From holy, Old English halig, whole, sound, set apart, with the adverbial -ly. The Greek hosios as an adverb means piously, in a manner answering to what is divinely sanctioned.
biblical_def: Defending his conduct at Thessalonica, Paul calls two witnesses and uses three adverbs: “Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:10). Holily is the adverb of holy, and the three words divide the whole of a minister's walk. Holily looks upward, to conduct answering to God's own holiness; justly looks outward, to what is owed to men; unblameably looks at the result, a life that affords no handle to an accuser. Paul appeals both to the Thessalonians, who had watched him, and to God, who had seen what they could not. The next verse shows the manner of it: “As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children” (1 Thessalonians 2:11). And the same letter grounds holy conduct in the divine call itself: “For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness” (1 Thessalonians 4:7). The adverb is therefore no boast. It is the ordinary expectation of a called man, and in the pastor it is also his credential, since an elder must be blameless.

corruption_summary: The separation of a minister's private life from his public gifts is accepted as normal, so that competence and influence are allowed to stand in the place of a holy walk.
corruption_paragraphs: A long series of ministry collapses has taught the evangelical world a bad habit: the gift is treated as the qualification. A man's preaching, reach or administrative skill is weighed, and his walk is treated as a private matter between him and his accountability group. On that account Paul's appeal in 1 Thessalonians 2:10 is pious autobiography rather than a stated standard.

Scripture makes the walk the qualification. The pastoral epistles list almost no skills and a great many characteristics, beginning with blameless; and Paul can summon both the congregation and God as witnesses to how he lived among them. Holily, justly, unblameably is not a claim to sinlessness, for the same apostle calls himself chief of sinners. It is a claim to a life open to inspection, and a church that stops requiring it will keep burying the consequences.

pos: adv. (in a manner that is received with favour; so as to please)
etymology: From acceptable, Latin acceptare, to receive willingly, with the adverbial -ly. The Greek euarestos means well-pleasing, from eu (well) and aresko (to please).
biblical_def: The great warning passage of Hebrews ends not in terror but in worship, and the worship has a stated manner: “Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear” (Hebrews 12:28). Acceptably means in the way God receives, and three things in the verse govern it. First, the ground is a gift: we are receiving a kingdom, so worship is response, never purchase. Second, the means is grace, which we are told to have, not to generate. Third, the manner is reverence and godly fear, and the writer immediately gives the reason: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). The clause rules out two opposite errors at once, a worship that presumes and a worship that despairs. Paul describes the same acceptable service in the language of sacrifice: “that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Romans 12:1). Acceptable worship is therefore not whatever the worshipper finds meaningful; it is what God has appointed, offered in grace and in fear.

corruption_summary: Acceptable worship is redefined as whatever the worshipper experiences as meaningful, so that God's appointment is replaced by the congregation's preference.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary worship talk is almost entirely subjective: what moved us, what we connected with, what felt authentic. On that account acceptability is measured at the human end, and the question of what God has commanded does not arise. The sincerity of the worshipper is held to settle the matter, and the vocabulary of experience crowds out the vocabulary of reverence and godly fear.

Hebrews 12:28 locates acceptability at the divine end and names the manner God requires. The dictionary holds the regulative principle of worship: what Scripture commands in corporate worship is required, and what Scripture has not commanded is not permitted. Far from making worship cold, this is what makes it safe and glad, for the verse grounds the whole duty in an unshakeable kingdom received as a gift and in grace supplied for the serving. And the reason given for reverence is not God's distance but His nature: our God is a consuming fire.

etymology: From several, Old French several, from Latin separ, separate, with the adverbial -ly. In older English severally means individually rather than numerously. The Greek is idia, each his own.
biblical_def: Closing his catalogue of spiritual gifts, Paul fixes their origin: “But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will” (1 Corinthians 12:11). Severally means individually, each his own, and the word guards two truths at once. The gifts are various and particular, distributed one by one; and the Giver is one and the same Spirit, acting as he will. Both halves cut against the Corinthian error. Those who despised lesser gifts are told that the Spirit assigned them; those who prized the showy gifts are told they did not choose their own. Paul states the purpose earlier in the chapter: “But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” (1 Corinthians 12:7), and he applies the same sovereignty to the body's very composition: “But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him” (1 Corinthians 12:18). The word therefore belongs with the dictionary's doctrine of the Spirit's free and sovereign distribution: no believer is giftless, no believer chose his gift, and no gift was given for its owner's display.

webster_full: SEVERALLY, adv. Separately; distinctly; apart from others.
SEVERAL, a. Separate; distinct; not common to two or more.

corruption_summary: Spiritual gifts are sought as marks of personal standing or pressed on all believers alike, when Scripture says the Spirit divides them individually as He wills.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors crowd this verse. The charismatic error makes a particular gift the required evidence of the Spirit's indwelling and teaches believers to seek it; Paul's severally as he will forbids any such uniform requirement, and his rhetorical questions at the end of the chapter assume that not all have the same gift. The opposite error treats gifting as personality or talent, a matter of self-discovery and self-deployment.

Paul's grammar settles both. The Spirit divides, the Spirit wills, God sets the members as it hath pleased Him. The believer's business is therefore not to acquire or to audition but to employ what has been assigned, and the stated purpose is to profit others, not to adorn oneself. That is why the chapter runs straight into the chapter on charity: a gift held severally is held for the body.

pos: n. (severity; keenness of rebuke or discipline)
etymology: From sharp, Old English scearp, cutting, with the suffix -ness. The Greek apotomos means abruptly, severely, literally cut off sheer, from apotemno, to cut away.
biblical_def: Paul closes his hardest letter with an explanation of why he wrote it before coming: “Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction” (2 Corinthians 13:10). Sharpness is severity, the Greek word picturing something cut off sheer. Three things in the verse govern pastoral severity. It is real: Paul has such power and could use it. It is a last resort: he writes beforehand precisely so that it may not be needed. And it is bounded by its purpose: the authority was given to edification, and not to destruction. He had said the same earlier: “For though I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed” (2 Corinthians 10:8). Nor is sharpness always to be withheld; Titus is commanded to it: “This witness is true. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). Church discipline in the Reformed tradition stands exactly here: severity in the service of soundness, never of ruin.

corruption_summary: Pastoral severity is either abandoned altogether as unloving or wielded without the limit Paul states, so that discipline becomes impossible in one church and destructive in the next.
corruption_paragraphs: The first failure is the common one. A therapeutic reading of ministry treats any rebuke as harm, and so church discipline quietly disappears: no sharpness, no correction, no removal of the unrepentant, and in the end no protection for the flock. Titus 1:13 stands against it with a command, not a permission.

The second failure is the abusive one, and it is the reason the first gains traction. Men have used authority to crush congregations, settle scores and secure compliance, and have cited Paul to do it. Paul himself closes that door in the same breath: the power was given to edification, and not to destruction. Severity that does not aim at the soundness of the one rebuked is not biblical sharpness but its counterfeit, and the elder who cannot tell the difference should not be trusted with either.

pos: adv. (archaic; in whatever respect, in whatsoever matter)
etymology: A compound of where, in and soever, on the pattern of whatsoever and whithersoever. The Authorized Version uses a family of such compounds to render Greek relatives with indefinite force.
biblical_def: In the middle of what he calls his foolish boasting, Paul concedes the ground to his critics and then takes it back: “I speak as concerning reproach, as though we had been weak. Howbeit whereinsoever any is bold, (I speak foolishly,) I am bold also” (2 Corinthians 11:21). Whereinsoever means in whatever respect, and the word is doing careful work. Paul will not grant that the super-apostles have any ground of boasting he lacks; in whatever particular they are bold, he can match it. But he brackets the whole performance with I speak foolishly, because boasting is beneath the gospel and he engages in it only to expose theirs. Two chapters later the real conclusion arrives, and it inverts everything: “If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities” (2 Corinthians 11:30), and then the Lord's own word to him: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The archaic adverb thus marks the hinge of the letter, where Paul grants the comparison in order to abolish the standard of comparison altogether.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): WHEREIN, in which; in what; WHERE-IN-SOEVER, in whatever respect or particular.
webster_full: WHEREIN, adv. In which; in which thing, time, respect or place.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Ministry is compared and ranked by impressiveness, the very standard Paul adopts ironically in order to destroy it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the one Paul's irony establishes: the comparison of ministers by impressiveness is a false measure, and he enters it only under protest, flagging his own words as foolish.

The false measure is thoroughly at home in the modern church. Platform, crowd, polish, credentials and personal magnetism are compared, ranked and envied, and the ranking is often sincere in its piety. Paul's answer is not to win the contest but to change the ledger: he boasts of beatings, shipwrecks, sleeplessness, a thorn he was not given leave to remove, and finally of infirmities, because the Lord said His strength is made perfect in weakness. Whereinsoever any is bold is an argument Paul makes in order never to have to make it again.
